slides.heading: Sound
slides.body_md: Part 1: how sound is made, how it travels, and how fast it goes.

visual.alt: Table of five sources of sound and what vibrates in each

slides.narration: Every sound that you hear comes from something that is vibrating. A drum, a string, a bell, even your own throat. In this part we find out how a vibration becomes a sound that reaches your ear, why sound needs a medium such as air to travel, and how to measure the speed and wavelength of sound.

slides.heading: Sound is produced by vibration
slides.body_md: A **vibration** is a rapid to-and-fro motion about a mean position. **Sound is produced by vibrating bodies.** When a tuning fork is struck and its prong touches a ball of thread, the ball is pushed away: this shows that the prong is vibrating. A vibrating body pushes and pulls on the air around it, and this disturbance spreads out as a **sound wave**. When the vibration stops, the sound stops.

rows: A struck tuning fork makes a hanging thread ball jump
Fingers on your throat feel a buzz when you speak
A hand on a drum stops the sound
Rice grains jump on a drum skin when the drum is struck

visual.alt: Table of four simple observations that show sound is produced by vibration

slides.narration: Sound is produced by vibration. A vibration is a quick to and fro motion about a fixed position. Strike a tuning fork and touch a hanging thread ball with it, and the ball jumps away. Touch your throat while you speak and you feel the buzz. Put your hand on a ringing drum, and the sound stops. When the vibration stops, the sound stops too.

slides.heading: Sound needs a medium
slides.body_md: Sound travels through a **medium**: a solid, a liquid or a gas. It **cannot** travel through a **vacuum**. In the bell jar experiment an electric bell hangs inside a sealed glass jar. As a vacuum pump removes the air, the sound of the bell grows fainter, although the hammer still strikes the gong. When air is let back, the sound grows loud again. This is why astronauts on the Moon, where there is no air, speak through radios.

nodes.label: Bell rings inside a sealed jar full of air: sound is loud
Pump removes the air: sound grows fainter
Almost no air left: hardly any sound, but the hammer still moves
Air is let in again: sound becomes loud once more

visual.alt: Flow showing the bell jar experiment: the sound fades as the air is removed and returns when air is let back

slides.narration: Sound needs a medium to travel. In the bell jar experiment, an electric bell rings inside a sealed glass jar. As the pump removes the air, the sound grows fainter, even though we can still see the hammer hitting the gong. When air is let back in, the sound returns. So sound cannot travel through empty space, a vacuum. This is why astronauts on the Moon need radios to talk.

slides.heading: Sound travels as a longitudinal wave
slides.body_md: As a vibrating body moves forward it **pushes** the air particles together, making a **compression** (C): a region of high pressure. As it moves back it leaves a region where the particles are spread out, a **rarefaction** (R): a region of low pressure. These regions move away from the source, but the air particles only vibrate **to and fro** about their places along the direction of travel of the wave. The distance between two successive compressions is the **wavelength** $\lambda$.

visual.alt: A sound wave in air as bands of compressions and rarefactions above the matching pressure graph, with the wavelength and amplitude marked
visual.caption: Compressions are high-pressure bands; rarefactions are low-pressure bands.

slides.narration: Look at the picture. The vertical lines stand for air particles. Where they crowd together we have a compression, with high pressure. Where they are spread out we have a rarefaction, with low pressure. These bands travel outward from the source. The air itself does not travel with the wave. Each particle only moves a little to and fro. The graph below shows the pressure rising at each compression and falling at each rarefaction.

slides.heading: Longitudinal and transverse waves
slides.body_md: In a **longitudinal wave** the particles of the medium vibrate **parallel** to the direction in which the wave travels. Sound in air is a longitudinal wave. In a **transverse wave**, such as a wave on a rope shaken up and down, the particles vibrate **at right angles** to the direction of travel. A longitudinal wave moves as compressions and rarefactions; a transverse wave moves as crests and troughs.

visual.alt: Table comparing longitudinal and transverse waves

slides.narration: There are two kinds of wave. In a longitudinal wave, the particles of the medium vibrate along the direction in which the wave moves. Sound in air is longitudinal, and it travels as compressions and rarefactions. In a transverse wave, the particles vibrate at right angles to the direction of travel, like a rope shaken up and down, and the pattern has crests and troughs.

slides.heading: Frequency, time period, amplitude and wavelength
slides.body_md: The **frequency** $f$ is the number of vibrations (or complete waves) per second; its unit is the **hertz** (Hz). The **time period** $T$ is the time for one complete vibration, in seconds, and $T = 1/f$. The **amplitude** $A$ is the maximum displacement of a vibrating particle from its mean position (on the pressure graph, the height of the wave above the normal level). The **wavelength** $\lambda$ is the distance between two successive compressions or two successive rarefactions, in metres.

rows: time for one vibration; T = 1 ÷ f
largest displacement from the mean position

visual.alt: Table of frequency, time period, amplitude and wavelength with their symbols, units and meanings

slides.narration: Four quantities describe a wave. The frequency is the number of vibrations in one second, measured in hertz. The time period is the time for one vibration, and it is one divided by the frequency. The amplitude is the largest displacement from the mean position. The wavelength is the distance between two successive compressions, or two successive rarefactions, measured in metres.

slides.heading: The relation v = f λ
slides.body_md:
In **one time period** $T$ the wave moves forward by **one wavelength** $\lambda$. So the speed of the wave is
$$v = \dfrac{\lambda}{T} = \lambda \times \dfrac{1}{T} = f\lambda$$
**Speed = frequency × wavelength.** In a given medium the speed of sound is fixed, so a sound of higher frequency has a **shorter** wavelength.

nodes.label: In one period T the wave moves one wavelength λ

visual.alt: Flow showing how the speed of a wave equals wavelength divided by time period, which equals frequency times wavelength

slides.narration: Here is how to derive the relation between speed, frequency and wavelength. In one time period the wave moves forward by exactly one wavelength. Speed is distance divided by time, so the speed is the wavelength divided by the time period. But one over the time period is the frequency. So the speed equals the frequency times the wavelength.

slides.heading: Worked example: wavelength of a whistle
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The whistle of a pressure cooker has a frequency of 2000 Hz. Taking the speed of sound in air as 344 m s⁻¹, find its wavelength and time period.

**Step 1.** $\lambda = v/f = 344 / 2000 = 0.172$ m.

**Step 2.** $T = 1/f = 1 / 2000 = 0.00050$ s, that is 0.5 millisecond.

**Check.** $f\lambda = 2000 \times 0.172 = 344$ m s⁻¹.

visual.alt: Table of the wavelength and time period of a 2000 hertz whistle

slides.narration: The whistle has a frequency of two thousand hertz, and sound in air travels at about three hundred forty-four metres per second. The wavelength is the speed divided by the frequency, which is seventeen point two centimetres, or point one seven two metres. The time period is one divided by the frequency, which is half a millisecond. Multiplying frequency by wavelength gives back the speed.

slides.heading: Speed of sound in solids, liquids and gases
slides.body_md: Sound travels fastest in **solids**, slower in **liquids** and slowest in **gases**, because the particles of a solid are packed close together and pass the vibration on quickly. The values below are approximate. The speed in a gas also **increases with temperature**: in air it is about 344 m s⁻¹ at about 22 °C and a little less on a cold day.

visual.alt: Table of the approximate speed of sound in air, sea water and steel

slides.narration: Sound travels fastest in solids, more slowly in liquids and slowest in gases. In air at room temperature it travels at about three hundred forty-four metres per second. In sea water the speed is about fifteen hundred metres per second, and in steel about five thousand. These are approximate values. In a gas the speed also rises as the temperature rises.

slides.heading: Worked example: sound through steel and air
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A student strikes one end of a 100 m steel pipe with a hammer. Her friend at the other end hears two sounds, one through the steel and one through the air. Find the time taken by each, taking 5000 m s⁻¹ in steel and 344 m s⁻¹ in air.

**Step 1.** Through steel: $t = d/v = 100 / 5000 = 0.020$ s.

**Step 2.** Through air: $t = 100 / 344 = 0.29$ s.

**Step 3.** The two sounds are about 0.27 s apart, long enough to hear separately. The sound through the steel arrives first.

visual.alt: Table of the time taken by sound to travel 100 metres through steel and through air

slides.narration: The time taken is the distance divided by the speed. Through the steel pipe, one hundred metres at five thousand metres per second takes only two hundredths of a second. Through the air it takes about twenty-nine hundredths of a second. So the friend hears the sound through the steel first, and the sound through the air a little later, about a quarter of a second after.

slides.heading: Worked example: how far is the lightning?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A flash of lightning is seen, and the thunder is heard 4.5 s later. How far away did the lightning strike? Take the speed of sound as 344 m s⁻¹ and treat the light as arriving at once.

**Step 1.** Distance $= vt = 344 \times 4.5 = 1548$ m.

**Step 2.** That is about 1.5 km.

visual.alt: Table of the distance of lightning for time gaps of 1.0, 3.0 and 4.5 seconds

slides.narration: Light is so fast that we see the flash almost at once, but sound takes time to arrive. The gap between the flash and the thunder tells us the distance. Four and a half seconds at three hundred forty-four metres per second is about fifteen hundred metres. So the lightning struck roughly one and a half kilometres away.

slides.narration: To sum up. Sound is produced by vibrating bodies and needs a medium to travel. In air it is a longitudinal wave of compressions and rarefactions. The frequency, time period, amplitude and wavelength describe the wave, and the speed equals frequency times wavelength. visual.alt: Table of the three characteristics of a sound, what each depends on and how we sense it

slides.narration: In this part we learn why a whistle sounds shrill and a drum sounds deep, why some sounds are loud and some soft, and how we can tell a flute from a violin. We study sounds that our ears cannot hear. Then we see how sound bounces from surfaces to make echoes, how bats and ships use echoes, and what C V Raman found about Indian drums.

slides.heading: Pitch, loudness and quality
slides.body_md: **Pitch** is how shrill or deep a sound seems. It depends on the **frequency**: a higher frequency gives a higher pitch. **Loudness** depends on the **amplitude**: a bigger amplitude (a harder strike, a bigger push of air) gives a louder sound. It is measured in **decibels** (dB). **Quality** (timbre) is what lets us tell two sounds of the same pitch and loudness apart, such as a flute and a violin. It depends on the **mixture of frequencies** the source produces: a main note and extra higher notes called **overtones**.

slides.narration: Pitch tells us whether a sound is shrill or deep. It depends on the frequency. A higher frequency means a higher pitch. Loudness depends on the amplitude, so a harder strike makes a louder sound. Quality lets us tell a flute from a violin even when both play the same note equally loudly. It depends on the mixture of higher notes, called overtones, that an instrument produces along with its main note.

slides.heading: Uses of ultrasound and infrasound
slides.body_md: **Ultrasound** has a very short wavelength, so it travels in narrow beams and reflects from small objects. Uses: **sonar** (finding the depth of the sea and shoals of fish), **medical scans** (pictures of the womb or the liver, and echo tests of the heart), **cleaning** delicate parts (watches, jewellery) in a bath of vibrating liquid, and **finding cracks** inside metal blocks. **Infrasound** is used by large animals such as elephants and whales to communicate over long distances.

slides.heading: Reflection of sound and echo
slides.body_md: Sound is **reflected** from a hard, flat surface such as a wall, a cliff or a stone building, just as light is reflected by a mirror. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. A reflected sound that we hear again is an **echo**. The sensation of a sound stays in the ear for about **0.1 s**, so to hear the echo **separately** it must reach the ear at least 0.1 s after the original. In that time the sound goes to the wall and back, so the minimum distance is $d = \dfrac{vt}{2} = \dfrac{344 \times 0.1}{2} = 17.2\ \text{m}$, about **17 m** in air.

slides.narration: Sound bounces back from a hard flat surface such as a wall or a cliff. A sound that we hear again after it bounces is called an echo. The ear holds on to a sound for about one tenth of a second, so the echo must come back at least one tenth of a second later to be heard separately. In that time sound travels there and back, so the wall must be at least about seventeen metres away.

slides.heading: Sonar: measuring depth with echoes
slides.body_md:
**Sonar** (sound navigation and ranging) uses ultrasound. A device on a boat sends out a short pulse, and the pulse is reflected from the sea bed. If the echo takes time $t$, the sound has travelled to the bottom **and back**, a distance $2d$. So $2d = vt$ and the depth is
$$d = \dfrac{vt}{2}$$
Here $d = \dfrac{1500 \times 1.2}{2} = 900$ m. Sonar also finds shoals of fish and sunken objects.

slides.heading: Worked example: echo distances
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** (a) Show that the least distance of a wall for a distinct echo is about 17 m. (b) A tourist claps near an old fort wall and hears the echo 0.80 s later. How far is the wall? Take 344 m s⁻¹.

**(a)** Minimum time $= 0.1$ s, so the sound travels $344 \times 0.1 = 34.4$ m there and back. The wall is half of this: $17.2$ m, about 17 m.

**(b)** Distance there and back $= 344 \times 0.80 = 275.2$ m. Distance of the wall $= 275.2 / 2 = 137.6$ m, about 138 m.

slides.narration: For a distinct echo the sound must return after at least one tenth of a second. In that time it travels about thirty-four metres, which is there and back, so the wall must be at least about seventeen metres away. For the fort wall, the echo comes after eight tenths of a second. That is two hundred seventy-five metres there and back, so the wall is about one hundred thirty-eight metres away.

slides.heading: Echolocation and reverberation
slides.body_md: **Echolocation:** bats and dolphins find their way and their prey by sending out ultrasound and listening to the echo. A bat gives out a series of very high-pitched squeaks; the echo from a moth tells it how far away the moth is and in which direction, so a bat can fly in the dark without hitting a wall. Dolphins send clicks in the water in the same way. **Reverberation:** in a large hall the sound is reflected again and again from the walls and ceiling, so it lingers and words blur. To reduce it, auditoriums use curtains, carpets, cushioned seats and perforated boards on the walls, which absorb sound.

slides.narration: Bats and dolphins use echolocation. A bat sends out squeaks of ultrasound and listens for the echo from an insect or a wall. The time and direction of the echo tell it where things are, so it can hunt in the dark. Dolphins do the same with clicks in water. In a big hall, repeated reflections cause reverberation, which blurs speech. Curtains, carpets and soft panels absorb the sound and reduce it.

slides.heading: C. V. Raman and Indian drums
slides.body_md: The Indian physicist **C. V. Raman** studied the sound of Indian musical instruments, especially the **tabla** and the **mridangam**. Most simple drums give overtones that are not related to the main note in a simple way, so they sound like a dull thud. Raman showed that in the tabla and the mridangam the **thick circular patch of special paste on the skin** (the "black spot") makes the overtones **harmonic**: they are whole-number multiples of the lowest frequency, $f$, $2f$, $3f$ and so on. This is why these drums give a clear musical note.

slides.heading: Worked example: wavelength of a bat call
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A bat sends out an ultrasound squeak of frequency 50 kHz. Find the wavelength in air (344 m s⁻¹) and the time period.

**Step 1.** $f = 50000$ Hz, so $\lambda = v/f = 344 / 50000 = 0.00688$ m $= 6.88$ mm.

**Step 2.** $T = 1/f = 1/50000 = 2.0 \times 10^{-5}$ s.

The wavelength is only about 7 mm, so the squeak can reflect from small objects such as a moth. A wave about a metre long would bend around such a small object instead of bouncing back.

slides.narration: A bat squeak has a frequency of fifty kilohertz, which is fifty thousand hertz. The wavelength is the speed divided by the frequency, which is about seven millimetres. This short wavelength means the sound can reflect from tiny objects like a moth. A long wave of about a metre would bend around such a small object, instead of bouncing back from it.

sections.heading: 1. Production of sound
sections.body_md:
**Sound is produced by vibrating bodies.** A vibration is a rapid to-and-fro motion about a mean position. A struck tuning fork makes a hanging thread ball jump; the throat buzzes when we speak; a drum skin makes rice grains dance. When the vibration stops, the sound stops.

A vibrating body disturbs the air around it. This disturbance spreads as a **sound wave** and reaches the ear.

key_terms.definition_md: A rapid to-and-fro motion about a mean position.
A disturbance produced by a vibrating body that travels through a medium as a wave.

visual.alt: Table of four sources of sound and what vibrates in each

sections.heading: 2. Propagation: a longitudinal wave that needs a medium
sections.body_md:
Sound needs a **medium** (solid, liquid or gas) and cannot travel through a **vacuum**: in the bell jar experiment the sound fades as the air is pumped out and returns when air is let in.

In air, sound is a **longitudinal wave**: the air particles vibrate **parallel** to the direction in which the wave travels. A **compression** (C) is a region where the particles are crowded together (high pressure); a **rarefaction** (R) is a region where they are spread apart (low pressure). The particles only vibrate about their places; the wave pattern moves on.

key_terms.definition_md: The material (solid, liquid or gas) through which a wave travels.
A wave in which the particles vibrate along the direction of travel of the wave.
A region of a sound wave where particles are close together and pressure is high.
A region of a sound wave where particles are far apart and pressure is low.

sections.heading: 3. Wave quantities and v = fλ
sections.body_md:
**Frequency** $f$: vibrations per second, in hertz (Hz). **Time period** $T = 1/f$, in seconds. **Amplitude**: the maximum displacement from the mean position. **Wavelength** $\lambda$: distance between two successive compressions (or rarefactions).

In one period the wave travels one wavelength, so
$$v = \dfrac{\lambda}{T} = f\lambda$$
In a given medium $v$ is fixed, so a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength. Example: $f = 2000$ Hz and $v = 344\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ give $\lambda = 0.172$ m.

key_terms.definition_md: Number of vibrations per second; unit hertz.
Time taken for one complete vibration, T = 1/f.
Maximum displacement of a vibrating particle from its mean position.
Distance between two successive compressions or two successive rarefactions.

sections.heading: 4. Speed of sound in different media
sections.body_md:
Sound travels fastest in **solids**, slower in **liquids** and slowest in **gases**. The values below are approximate: air about 344 m s⁻¹ (at about 22 °C), sea water about 1500 m s⁻¹, steel about 5000 m s⁻¹. In a gas the speed increases as the temperature rises.

Time taken $= \text{distance} / \text{speed}$. Over 100 m, sound takes about 0.02 s in steel and about 0.29 s in air.

key_terms.definition_md: Distance travelled by a sound wave per second; it depends on the medium and its temperature.

sections.heading: 5. Pitch, loudness, quality and the range of hearing
sections.body_md:
**Pitch** depends on frequency (higher frequency, higher pitch). **Loudness** depends on amplitude and is measured in decibels (dB). **Quality** (timbre) depends on the mixture of **overtones** and lets us tell two instruments apart.

The audible range of the human ear is about **20 Hz to 20 kHz**. Below 20 Hz is **infrasound** (used by elephants and whales); above 20 kHz is **ultrasound**. Ultrasound is used in sonar, medical scans, cleaning and finding flaws in metal.

key_terms.definition_md: How shrill or deep a sound seems; depends on frequency.
How loud a sound seems; depends on amplitude.
The characteristic that lets us tell sounds of the same pitch and loudness apart; depends on overtones.

sections.heading: 6. Reflection, echo, sonar, echolocation and Raman
sections.body_md:
Sound is reflected from hard, flat surfaces. An **echo** is a reflected sound heard separately; it must arrive at least about **0.1 s** after the original, so the reflector must be at least $d = vt/2 = 344 \times 0.1/2 \approx 17$ m away in air. **Reverberation** is the lingering of sound in a hall due to repeated reflections; curtains, carpets and perforated boards reduce it.

**Sonar** uses ultrasound: depth $d = vt/2$ (the sound goes down and back). **Echolocation:** bats and dolphins find their way and prey by the echoes of their ultrasound.

**C. V. Raman** studied the sound of Indian drums such as the tabla and the mridangam and showed that the loaded (black-patch) skin gives **harmonic overtones**, whole-number multiples of the lowest frequency.

key_terms.definition_md: A reflected sound that is heard separately from the original sound.
The persistence of sound in a hall because of repeated reflections.
A device that uses ultrasound echoes to find the depth of water or to locate objects under water.

notes.exam_tips_md:

- Write v = fλ first; convert kHz to Hz; give the unit of the answer.

cards.front_md: How is sound produced?
cards.back_md: By a vibrating body.

cards.front_md: What is a vibration?
cards.back_md: A rapid to-and-fro motion about a mean position.

cards.front_md: What does the bell jar experiment show?
cards.back_md: Sound needs a medium: it fades as the air is pumped out and cannot travel through a vacuum.

cards.front_md: Why must astronauts on the Moon use radios to talk?
cards.back_md: There is no air on the Moon, so sound cannot travel between them.

cards.front_md: What kind of wave is sound in air?
cards.back_md: A longitudinal wave: the particles vibrate along the direction in which the wave travels.

cards.front_md: What is a compression?
cards.back_md: A region of a sound wave where the particles are crowded together and the pressure is high.

cards.front_md: What is a rarefaction?
cards.back_md: A region of a sound wave where the particles are spread apart and the pressure is low.

cards.front_md: How do transverse waves differ from longitudinal waves?
cards.back_md: In a transverse wave the particles vibrate at right angles to the direction of travel (crests and troughs).

cards.front_md: Define frequency and give its unit.
cards.back_md: The number of vibrations per second; the hertz (Hz).

cards.front_md: Define time period and write its relation with frequency.
cards.back_md: The time for one complete vibration, in seconds; $T = 1/f$.

cards.front_md: Define amplitude.
cards.back_md: The maximum displacement of a vibrating particle from its mean position.

cards.front_md: Define wavelength.
cards.back_md: The distance between two successive compressions or two successive rarefactions.

cards.front_md: Derive the relation between v, f and λ in one line.
cards.back_md: In one period $T$ the wave moves one wavelength, so $v = \lambda/T = f\lambda$.

cards.front_md: A sound has f = 2000 Hz in air (344 m/s). Wavelength?
In which state of matter does sound travel fastest?
cards.back_md: In solids, then liquids, and slowest in gases.

cards.front_md: Approximate speeds of sound in air, sea water and steel?
cards.back_md: About 344 m/s, about 1500 m/s and about 5000 m/s.

cards.front_md: How does temperature affect the speed of sound in air?
cards.back_md: The speed increases as the temperature rises.

cards.front_md: What does pitch depend on?
cards.back_md: On frequency: a higher frequency gives a higher pitch.

cards.front_md: What does loudness depend on?
cards.back_md: On amplitude: a larger amplitude gives a louder sound.

cards.front_md: What is the unit of loudness?
cards.back_md: The decibel (dB).

cards.front_md: What is the quality (timbre) of a sound?
cards.back_md: The characteristic that lets us tell two sounds of the same pitch and loudness apart; it depends on the overtones.

cards.front_md: What is the audible range of the human ear?
cards.back_md: About 20 Hz to 20 kHz.

cards.front_md: Define infrasound.
cards.back_md: Sound of frequency below 20 Hz, which humans cannot hear.

cards.front_md: Define ultrasound.
cards.back_md: Sound of frequency above 20 kHz, which humans cannot hear.

cards.front_md: Name three uses of ultrasound.
cards.back_md: Sonar, medical scans and cleaning delicate parts (also finding cracks in metal).

cards.front_md: What is an echo?
cards.back_md: A reflected sound that is heard separately from the original sound.

cards.front_md: What is the minimum distance of the reflector for an echo in air?
cards.back_md: About 17 m: $d = vt/2 = 344 \times 0.1/2 \approx 17$ m.

cards.front_md: Why is the depth found with sonar given by d = vt/2?
cards.back_md: The pulse travels down and back up, so the distance travelled is twice the depth.

cards.front_md: What is echolocation?
cards.back_md: Locating objects by the echoes of ultrasound, as bats and dolphins do.

cards.front_md: What is reverberation and how is it reduced?
cards.back_md: The lingering of sound in a hall due to repeated reflections; reduced by curtains, carpets and perforated boards.

cards.front_md: What did C. V. Raman study about Indian drums?
cards.back_md: He studied the tabla and the mridangam and showed that their loaded skins give harmonic overtones, which makes a clear musical note.

cards.front_md: What does "harmonic overtones" mean?
cards.back_md: Overtones whose frequencies are whole-number multiples of the lowest frequency: $f$, $2f$, $3f$ and so on.

questions.stem_md: Two astronauts stand side by side on the surface of the Moon, where there is no air. Without their radios, they:

options.text_md: cannot hear each other, because there is no medium to carry the sound
can hear each other normally, because they are close together
can hear each other faintly, if they shout
can hear each other, because sound travels through the ground in their boots

questions.solution_md: Sound needs a material medium and cannot travel through a vacuum. With no air between them, the sound of a voice cannot reach the other astronaut — option (a). Their radios work with radio waves, not sound.

questions.stem_md: A drummer strikes a tabla and a clear note is heard. The note is produced because the stretched skin of the tabla:

options.text_md: moves steadily in one direction
becomes hot
stops moving after the strike
vibrates to and fro about its mean position

questions.solution_md: Sound is produced by vibrating bodies. The struck skin moves to and fro and passes the disturbance to the air — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Sound can travel through all of the following EXCEPT:

options.text_md: a steel rail
sea water
a vacuum
air

questions.solution_md: Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a medium (solid, liquid or gas). A vacuum has no particles to vibrate, so sound cannot travel through it — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A sound wave travels through air from left to right. The air particles vibrate:

options.text_md: to and fro along the left–right direction
up and down, at right angles to the left–right direction
in circles around the source
only towards the right, travelling along with the wave

questions.solution_md: Sound in air is a longitudinal wave: the particles vibrate parallel to the direction in which the wave moves, but they only oscillate about their positions and do not travel with the wave — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A rarefaction in a sound wave in air is a region in which the air particles are:

options.text_md: close together, and the pressure is higher than normal
far apart, and the pressure is higher than normal
far apart, and the pressure is lower than normal
close together, and the pressure is lower than normal

questions.solution_md: In a rarefaction the particles are spread out, so the pressure falls below the normal value — option (c). A compression is the opposite.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The sound of an electric bell inside a sealed glass jar becomes fainter as the air is pumped out.

**Reason (R):** Sound is a wave that needs a material medium to travel.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: As the air is removed there are fewer particles to carry the vibrations to the glass, so the sound fades. R states why this happens, so it explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The air pressure in a compression is higher than the normal pressure.

**Reason (R):** In a compression the air particles are crowded closer together than normal.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Crowding the particles together raises the pressure, so R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Sound waves in air are longitudinal waves.

**Reason (R):** In a longitudinal wave the particles of the medium vibrate at right angles to the direction of travel of the wave.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: in a longitudinal wave the particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel. Vibration at right angles describes a transverse wave — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Sound travels slowest in solids, faster in liquids and fastest in gases.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases, because the particles of a solid are closest together.

questions.stem_md: Sound waves in air are called ___ waves because the particles vibrate along the direction in which the wave travels.
questions.solution_md: They are **longitudinal** waves, made of compressions and rarefactions.

questions.stem_md: In the bell jar experiment the sound of a ringing bell fades as the air is pumped out, although the bell can still be seen ringing. What does this show about sound?

answer.model_answer_md: It shows that sound needs a material medium to travel. As the air is removed, fewer particles are left to carry the vibrations from the bell to the glass wall, so the sound grows fainter. In a vacuum there is no medium, so sound cannot travel at all.

questions.solution_md: Sound needs a medium; it cannot travel through a vacuum.

marking_scheme.step: Fewer particles carry the vibrations, none in a vacuum

questions.stem_md: Explain what happens to the air particles when a sound wave passes through air. Name the high-pressure and low-pressure regions formed.

answer.model_answer_md: The vibrating source pushes the nearby air particles together and then moves back, so the particles are alternately crowded and spread out. The crowded high-pressure regions are compressions and the spread-out low-pressure regions are rarefactions. The particles only vibrate to and fro about their places.

questions.solution_md: Compressions (high pressure) and rarefactions (low pressure); particles vibrate about fixed positions.

marking_scheme.step: Compressions are crowded high-pressure regions and rarefactions are spread-out low-pressure regions
Particles only vibrate to and fro; the wave moves on

questions.stem_md: Describe how sound travels from a vibrating tuning fork to your ear. Name the type of wave and the two kinds of region in it.

answer.model_answer_md: The prongs of the fork vibrate and push the air near them, making a compression, and then pull back, leaving a rarefaction. These regions travel outward through the air as a wave. Sound is a longitudinal wave, because the air particles vibrate along the direction of travel. When the wave reaches the ear, the air vibrates the eardrum, and we hear the sound.

questions.solution_md: Compressions and rarefactions travel as a longitudinal wave to the ear.

marking_scheme.step: Vibration makes compressions and rarefactions in the air
A longitudinal wave: particles vibrate along the direction of travel
The wave reaches the ear and makes the eardrum vibrate

questions.stem_md:
(a) How is sound produced? Give two examples.

(b) Describe the bell jar experiment and state what it shows.

(c) Explain how a sound wave moves through air, using the terms compression and rarefaction.

answer.model_answer_md: Sound is produced by vibrating bodies, for example a plucked veena string and a struck tabla skin. In the bell jar experiment an electric bell rings inside a sealed jar. As a pump removes the air, the sound becomes fainter and it fades almost to nothing, although the bell can still be seen working. When air is let in the sound returns. This shows that sound needs a medium and cannot travel through a vacuum. In air the vibrating source pushes the particles together, forming a compression with high pressure, and then leaves a region where they are spread out, a rarefaction with low pressure. These regions travel on as a longitudinal wave.

questions.solution_md: Vibration examples; bell jar and conclusion; compressions and rarefactions of a longitudinal wave.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Bell jar experiment and the conclusion that sound needs a medium
(c) Compressions and rarefactions travelling as a longitudinal wave

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md:
A student produces three notes on a musical instrument in a room where the speed of sound is 344 m s⁻¹, and measures the frequency and the wavelength of each.

| Note | Frequency (Hz) | Wavelength in air (m) |
|---|---|---|
| A | 172 | 2.0 |
| B | 344 | 1.0 |
| C | 860 | 0.40 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (a) Note C, because it has the highest frequency

**(b)** $v = f\lambda = 172 \times 2.0 = 344\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

**(c)** (i) $\lambda = v/f = 344 / 688 = 0.50$ m.

**OR** (ii) The wavelength becomes shorter as the frequency increases: 2.0 m at 172 Hz, 1.0 m at 344 Hz and 0.40 m at 860 Hz. The speed of sound is fixed in the same air, and since v = fλ, a larger f must go with a smaller λ.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Pitch depends on frequency, and note C has the greatest frequency, 860 Hz — option (a). The speed of sound is the same for all three notes in the same air.

**(b)** v = fλ = 344 m/s.

**(c)** (i) λ = v ÷ f = 0.50 m.

(ii) Speed is fixed, so f and λ are inversely related.

alternatives.solution_md: Speed is fixed, so f and λ are inversely related.

Speed is constant, so f × λ is constant

questions.stem_md: A sound of frequency 172 Hz travels in air at 344 m s⁻¹. Its wavelength is:
questions.solution_md: $\lambda = v/f = 344/172 = 2.0$ m — option (c). (a) divides frequency by speed, (b) adds them and (d) multiplies them.

questions.stem_md: A sound travels through a steel rail, through water and through air. The correct order, from the fastest to the slowest, is:

options.text_md: air, water, steel rail
water, steel rail, air
steel rail, air, water
steel rail, water, air

questions.solution_md: Sound is fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases: about 5000 m/s in steel, about 1500 m/s in water and about 344 m/s in air — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A tuning fork vibrates 250 times in one second. Its time period is:
A note of frequency 400 Hz is replaced by a note of frequency 800 Hz in the same air. The wavelength of the sound:

options.text_md: becomes twice as large
stays the same
becomes four times as large
becomes half as large

questions.solution_md: In the same air $v$ is constant, and $\lambda = v/f$. Doubling $f$ halves $\lambda$ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A dhol player strikes the drum harder. The sound becomes louder because the amplitude of the vibration of the skin:

options.text_md: decreases
increases
stays the same, but the frequency increases
stays the same, but the wavelength decreases

questions.solution_md: Loudness depends on the amplitude of the vibration. A harder strike makes the skin vibrate with a larger amplitude — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The number of vibrations made per second by a vibrating body is called its ___.
questions.solution_md: It is the **frequency**, measured in hertz.

questions.stem_md: A nadaswaram player sounds a note of frequency 600 Hz. Taking the speed of sound in air as 344 m s⁻¹, find the wavelength of the sound, in m.
A sound wave in air has a wavelength of 0.25 m. Taking the speed of sound as 344 m s⁻¹, find its frequency, in Hz.
A stretched wire on a sitar makes 1800 complete vibrations in 5.0 s. Find the frequency of the sound it produces, in Hz.
questions.solution_md: Frequency $=$ number of vibrations $\div$ time $= 1800 / 5 = 360$ Hz. (The time period is $1/360 = 0.00278$ s.)

questions.stem_md: A steel rail is 250 m long. A man strikes one end with a hammer and a girl at the other end hears the sound twice, once through the rail and once through the air. Taking 5000 m s⁻¹ in steel and 344 m s⁻¹ in air, find the time gap between the two sounds, in s.

marking_scheme.step: Times 0.050 s in steel and 0.727 s in air

questions.solution_md: Distance $= vt = 344 \times 8.0 = 2752$ m $= 2.75$ km.

questions.stem_md: Define the time period of a wave. A sound has a frequency of 250 Hz. Write its time period and say what the wave does in one time period.

answer.model_answer_md: The time period is the time taken for one complete vibration. For a frequency of 250 Hz it is $T = 1/f = 1/250 = 0.004$ s. In one time period the wave moves forward by a distance of one wavelength.

questions.solution_md: T = 1/f = 0.004 s; the wave moves one wavelength.

marking_scheme.step: The wave advances one wavelength in one period

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define frequency, time period, amplitude and wavelength of a sound wave.

(b) Derive the relation v = fλ.

(c) A sound of frequency 500 Hz travels in air (344 m s⁻¹) and in steel (5000 m s⁻¹). Find its wavelength in each.

answer.model_answer_md: Frequency is the number of vibrations per second. The time period is the time for one vibration, $T = 1/f$. The amplitude is the largest displacement from the mean position. The wavelength is the distance between two successive compressions or rarefactions. In one time period the wave moves one wavelength, so $v = \lambda/T = f\lambda$. In (c) the frequency stays the same, so in air $\lambda = 344/500 = 0.688$ m and in steel $\lambda = 5000/500 = 10$ m.

questions.solution_md: Four definitions; v = λ/T = fλ; 0.688 m in air and 10 m in steel.

marking_scheme.step: (b) One period gives one wavelength, so v = fλ
(c) 0.688 m in air and 10 m in steel

questions.stem_md: Which of these sounds is in the audible range of a healthy human ear?

options.text_md: a sound of frequency 10 Hz
a dog-whistle sound of frequency 25 000 Hz
a note of frequency 3000 Hz
a bat squeak of frequency 50 000 Hz

questions.solution_md: The audible range is about 20 Hz to 20 kHz. Only 3000 Hz lies inside it — option (c). 10 Hz is infrasound; 25 kHz and 50 kHz are ultrasound.

questions.stem_md: A thin veena string gives a higher note than a thick string of the same length. The thin string:

options.text_md: vibrates with a larger amplitude
produces a sound of greater speed
vibrates with a higher frequency
vibrates with a longer time period

questions.solution_md: Pitch depends on frequency. The thinner string vibrates faster, so its frequency is higher and its time period is shorter — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A harmonium and a flute play the same note at the same loudness. A listener can still tell them apart because of the difference in their:

options.text_md: quality, since the mixtures of overtones are different
pitch, since the frequencies are different
loudness, since the amplitudes are different
speed, since the waves travel at different speeds

questions.solution_md: The pitch (frequency) and loudness (amplitude) are the same. The quality, which depends on the overtones present, is different — option (a). The speed in the same air is the same.

questions.stem_md: A sound of frequency 12 Hz is:

options.text_md: ultrasound, which a human cannot hear
infrasound, which a human cannot hear
audible, but very loud
audible, but very faint

questions.solution_md: The audible range begins at about 20 Hz. A frequency below this is infrasound — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A sound of frequency 30 kHz is called:

options.text_md: infrasound
ultrasound
audible sound
a shock wave

questions.solution_md: Sound above about 20 kHz is ultrasound — option (b).

**Assertion (A):** A sound of frequency 15 Hz cannot be heard by a human being.

Choose the correct option.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true because 15 Hz is below the audible range. R is false: 15 Hz is infrasound; ultrasound is above 20 kHz — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Ultrasound is used in sonar to find the depth of the sea.

**Reason (R):** Ultrasound is sound of frequency above about 20 kHz.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but R only defines ultrasound. It does not explain why it is used for sonar, which is that its short wavelength allows narrow beams that reflect well — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The loudness of a sound depends on the frequency of the vibration and not on its amplitude.

options.text_md: True
False

options.text_md: Pitch of a sound
Loudness of a sound
Quality of a sound
Speed of a wave

questions.solution_md: Pitch goes with frequency, loudness with amplitude, quality with overtones, and speed equals fλ.

Infrasound is below and ultrasound is above this range

A sound of 40 kHz is ultrasound and cannot be heard.
